vignette:
Kwame is seventy-seven years old. He wakes before dawn, as he has every day for the past forty-three years. The alarm is not set. It does not need to be. His body learned a rhythm in the refugee camp that never left him—up before the light, when the world is still dangerous enough to be quiet.

He remembers the night the soldiers came. He was thirty-four then, a junior engineer at a telecommunications office in Accra. The elections had turned. His ethnic group was being purged from the civil service. They came to his house at 2 a.m., three young men in fatigues, carrying machetes and a list. Kwame escaped through the back window as his wife, Adwoa, hid in the latrine. He ran through the compound, past the neighbor’s burning kiosk, and did not stop until he reached the bush. He did not see his father again. Later, he learned his father had been taken to the police station and never returned.

For eleven months they lived in a refugee camp in Togo. The camp smelled of smoke, of too many bodies, of boiled cassava and despair. Kwame taught himself to sleep in two-hour intervals, listening for footsteps. He kept his few belongings—a pen, a notebook, his wedding ring—in a plastic bag tied to his waist. He learned to read faces for threat, to map exits from any tent. Those skills were survival then. They are a cage now.

After resettlement in the United States, Kwame rebuilt his life with the same precision he had once applied to writing code. He earned a certification, then a job at a small tech firm outside Minneapolis. He wrote clean, efficient software, modules that solved problems logically, step by step. For twenty-nine years he arrived early, stayed late, and never took his break in the noisy cafeteria. He debugged code the way he debugged his own mind—by isolating variables, eliminating noise. But trauma is not a bug. It does not follow syntax.

Now he is retired. Adwoa is still with him. Their three children are grown. The house is quiet. But quiet is not peace. A car backfires on the street, and Kwame’s coffee cup freezes halfway to his lips. His heart pounds; his hands shake. He does not spill—he never spills—but the memory floods in: the sound of gunfire, the smell of burning rubber, the wet heat of the bush at night. He tells himself it is only a truck. He does not believe it.

He avoids the local market on Saturdays because the crowd reminds him of the camp. He cannot watch news about political violence anywhere—not Africa, not Europe, not even a protest in the next state—because his chest tightens and he feels the old panic, the urge to run. He has not said the word “refugee” aloud in five years. When a well-meaning neighbor asked about his accent, Kwame said he was from Ghana and changed the subject. He no longer visits his father’s grave, because there is no grave.

At night he checks the locks three times. Adwoa sleeps beside him, but he lies awake, listening. He keeps a small flashlight and a spare key under his pillow. He knows it is irrational. He cannot stop. When a leaf falls against the window, he sees a soldier’s shadow.

His mind, once so orderly, now loops the same scenes: the sound of the list being read, his father’s name called out, the machete blade catching moonlight. He tries to overwrite the memory with code—if-then-else logic, a subroutine that skips the worst part. But the loop never exits. He cannot compile around what happened.

Sometimes Adwoa reaches for his hand. He lets her hold it, but he does not squeeze back. He wants to. He knows he should. But something inside him has learned that love makes you weak, that attachment gets you killed. So he sits in the dark of his own living room, a man who debugged systems for thirty years and cannot fix a single line of his own story.
